div.p: Objective Using qualitative and quantitative magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) features, this study aimed to distinguish between isocitrate dehydrogenase (IDH)-mutant astrocytomas (IDH-mA) and IDH-wildtype glioblastomas (IDH-wG) based on the fifth edition of the World Health Organization's (WHO's) classification of central nervous system (CNS) tumors (WHO CNS5), published in 2021.

div.head: Methods
div.p: We enrolled 87 IDH-mA and 102 IDH-wG patients with pathologically confirmed disease according to the WHO CNS5 standard. Pretreatment brain MRI images and genetic information were obtained for each patient. Qualitative imaging features were assessed, including the side of lesion center, multifocality/multicentricity, hemorrhage, pial invasion, ependymal invasion, cortical involvement, midline location invasion, and enhancement mode. The quantitative imaging features assessed included tumor volume-related metrics and the relative apparent diffusion coefficient (rADC)-related metrics based on tumor segmentation. Contrast-enhanced and non-enhanced areas of the tumors were analyzed separately. univariable analysis and logistic regression were used to select the candidate predictors. The discrimination performance of the logistic regression model was evaluated using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC). Internal validation was performed using the bootstrap approach.

div.head: Results
div.p: In terms of the qualitative features, IDH-mA exhibited less multifocality/ multicentricity (p = 0.032), more hemorrhage (p = 0.009), and more cortical involvement (p = 0.009) than IDH-wG. Regarding the quantitative imaging features, IDH-mA demonstrated higher values in V all (p = 0.001), V ne (p < 0.001), rmaxADC ce (p < 0.001), rminADC ne (p = 0.015), rmaxADC ne (p = 0.004), and rmeanADC all (p = 0.001) than IDH-wG. In the multivariable analysis of all patients, multifocality/multicentricity (odds ratio [OR] = 2.87, p = 0.033), V ne (OR = 1.02, p = 0.049), and rmaxADC ce (OR = 2.82, p < 0.001) were independent predictive factors for distinguishing IDH-mA from IDH-wG. A combination of multifocality/multicentricity, V ne , and rmaxADC ce (model) had a superior performance in distinguishing IDH-mA from IDH-wG, with an AUC, accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity of 0.849 (95% confidence interval [CI], 0.791-0.908), 76.5%, 66.3%, and 92.3%, respectively.

div.head: Background
div.p: Gliomas are the most common primary malignant brain tumors of the central nervous system (CNS), characterized by their invasive and diffusely infiltrative nature, with an incidence of about six cases per 100,000 individuals annually [1,2]. According to the fifth edition of the World Health Organization's (WHO's) classification of CNS tumors (WHO CNS5), isocitrate dehydrogenase (IDH) mutant diffuse astrocytic tumors are classified as IDH-mutant astrocytomas (IDH-mA), while IDH-wildtype astrocytomas and glioblastomas are collectively classified as IDH-wildtype glioblastomas (IDH-wG) [3]. Research has shown that IDH-mutant gliomas exhibit distinct biological behaviors and better survival rates compared to IDH-wildtype tumors for grade 4 gliomas [4,5]. IDH mutations are important as prognostic markers and for the molecular diagnosis of adult-type diffuse gliomas, highlighting the necessity for accurate preoperative assessments to guide personalized treatment.

Immunohistochemical analyses and exome sequencing are considered the gold standard for determining IDH mutation status in gliomas [6]. However, these methods are invasive, expensive, and susceptible to sampling bias due to factors like tissue heterogeneity and varying antigen levels [7]. Additionally, neurosurgical interventions may not always be feasible due to the location of these tumors, highlighting the urgency for non-invasive alternatives.

Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) plays an important role in the preoperative classification of gliomas and the optimization of treatment [8]. It offers reliable diagnosis by providing spatial and functional information, particularly through advanced techniques like diffusionweighted imaging (DWI). Morphological features, such as edema, necrosis, cysts, and enhancement, can be used to predict the molecular status and clinical outcome of patients with gliomas [9][10][11]. Additionally, qualitative features, such as noncontrast-enhancing components, are more prevalent in IDH-mutant gliomas and are associated with better survival outcomes [12]. DWI assesses the apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) to reflect tumor cellularity and may assist in distinguishing glioma grades and IDH genotypes [13][14][15]. Although numerous studies are currently investigating the detection of IDH status in gliomas, these studies are predominantly based on radiomics methods and more complicated MRI techniques [16][17][18][19], which cannot be widely applied in clinical practice. erefore, the aim of this study was to investigate the potential utility of qualitative and quantitative MRI features-which are widely accessible and universally obtainable from preoperative conventional and postcontrast images-in differentiating IDH-mA from IDH-wG.

div.head: Participants
div.p: We retrospectively identified adult patients diagnosed with grade 4 adult-type diffuse gliomas diagnosed in our hospital between June 2018 and September 2023. We reviewed these patients' clinical, radiological, histological, and molecular characteristics. is retrospective study was approved by the Ethical Review Committee of our hospital (Approval No. KYLL2024990). e requirement for informed consent was waived. A total of 527 consecutive patients whose histopathologic diagnoses were confirmed grade 4 adult-type diffuse gliomas were initially considered. After excluding 338 patients according to the exclusion criteria, a total of 189 patients were included in our study. e patient selection and classification flowchart is shown in Fig. 1.

Patients with the following inclusion criteria were studied: (1) pathological diagnosis of IDH-mA or IDH-wG confirmed by biopsy or surgical resection according to the WHO CNS5 classification; (2) age equal to or greater than 18 years; (3) no treatment had been performed before the MRI; and (4) completion of both conventional and contrast-enhanced MRI, including DWI-ADC, before surgery. e exclusion criteria were as follows: (1) secondary or recurrent IDH-mA or IDH-wG; (2) missing MRI sequences; (3) poor image quality due to examination procedures; and (4) missing/incomplete histopathological information. As a result, a total of 189 patients were included in the study.

div.head: MRI protocol
div.p: All MRI examinations were performed on 3.0-T MRI scanners (Discovery MR 750, Discovery MR 750w, SIGNA Pioneer; GE Healthcare).

e MRI protocols included T1-weighted imaging (T1WI), T2-weighted imaging (T2WI), T2 fluid attenuation inversion recovery (T2-FLAIR), contrast-enhanced T1WI (CE-T1WI), and DWI. ADC maps were generated automatically from DWI datasets by the MRI post-processing workstation acquired with b-values of 0 and 1000 s/mm 2 .
e MRI scan parameters are shown in Supplementary Table S1. All MRI data were extracted from the picture archiving and communication system and de-identified for further analysis.

div.head: Histopathological and molecular analysis
div.p: All surgical specimens were preserved using paraffin. IDH and other molecular statuses, including x-linked alpha-thalassemia/mental retardation syndrome (ATRX), TP53, and Ki-67, were determined by targeted nextgeneration sequencing, polymerase chain reaction sequencing, or immunohistochemistry and fluorescence in situ hybridization, respectively. Final diagnoses were established by integrating the histopathological and genetic test results in accordance with the WHO CNS5 classification.

div.head: Qualitative features analysis
div.p: Images were reviewed by two experienced neuroradiologists who were blinded to the pathological diagnoses.

ese neuroradiologists independently analyzed the preoperative MRI scans of patients within the institutional cohort. ey were tasked with determining the following metrics for each MRI scan: the side of lesion center (center/bilateral, left, or right), multifocality/multicentricity (yes or no), hemorrhage (yes or no), pial invasion (yes or no), ependymal invasion (yes or no), cortical involvement (yes or no), midline location invasion (yes or no), and enhancement mode (absence, faint and patchy, nodular, or ring-like).

e side of lesion center was considered the tumor epicenter. Multifocality was defined as the presence of at least two distinct regions of the glioma, completely separated by normal-appearing brain tissue. Multicentric lesions were characterized by distinct foci widely separated across different lobes or hemispheres. Hemorrhage was identified by intrinsic foci of low signal intensity on T2WI or high signal intensity on T1WI. Pial invasion was defined as the enhancement of the overlying pia mater in continuity with either enhanced or non-enhanced tumor tissue. Ependymal invasion was characterized by the involvement of adjacent ependymal surfaces continuous with the enhanced or non-enhanced tumor matrix. Cortical involvement refers to the extension of the tumor into the cortical mantle, whether enhancing or nonenhancing, or when the cortex was indistinguishable from the underlying tumor. Midline locations included structures such as the corpus callosum, thalamus, hypothalamus, basal ganglia, midbrain, pons, medulla, or cerebellum. Contrast enhancement was defined as increased signal intensity on postcontrast T1WI compared to precontrast T1WI images. Non-enhancing tumors exhibited increased signal intensity on T2WI (lower than that of cerebrospinal fluid) and decreased intensity on T1WI, often accompanied by mass effect and structural distortion, including blurring at the gray-white matter interface. On postcontrast T1WI, enhancement patterns were classified as follows: absence of enhancement indicated no discernible signal intensity increase within the tumor; faint and patchy enhancement comprised ill-defined, subtle areas of mild enhancement scattered throughout the lesion; nodular enhancement consisted of one or more well-circumscribed, rounded foci of enhancement; and ring-like enhancement was recognized as a thick, irregular rim of enhancement surrounding a central nonenhancing necrotic core.
After independent data collection, the interobserver agreement was calculated, and discordant results were resolved by consensus.

div.head: Image preprocessing and tumor segmentation
div.p: Image preprocessing and tumor segmentation were conducted using 3D Slicer Software (version 5.6.2, h t t p s : / / w w w . s l i c e r . o r g ) . T2-FLAIR and ADC images were c o -r e g i s t e r e d with CE-T1WI images to correct for sequence shifts caused by patient head movement during MRI scanning.

is ensured that MRI images from the three sequences for each patient were aligned on the same slice. e coregistered structural MRI images served as references for regions of interest (ROI) delineation. e delineation of the entire tumor region, including the parenchyma, infiltrating tumor, cystic areas, necrotic regions, and edema, was performed using T2-FLAIR images. e delineation of the enhanced tumor lesions was conducted on CE-T1WI images, specifically excluding macroscopic cystic, necrotic, dural, vascular, and hemorrhagic areas. e ROI for the entire tumor (ROI all ) was transferred to the CE-T1WI images, from which the ROI for the enhanced tumor (ROI ce ) was subtracted to derive the ROI for the non-enhanced tumor (ROI ne ). Subsequently, ROI all , ROI ce , and ROI ne were transferred to the co-registered ADC maps for independent analysis.

ROIs were manually drawn by a younger reader (with 5 years of experience) for all tumors in a random order. Another senior reader, a board-certified neuroradiologist (with 18 years of experience), confirmed the final and proper placement of ROIs. Both readers were blinded to patients' demographics and tumor molecular status. In patients with multiple lesions, the largest lesion was selected for segmentation and analysis.
e tumor segmentation diagram is presented in Fig. 2.

div.head: Quantitative features analysis
div.p: e volumes of the entire tumor (V all ), the enhanced tumor (V ce ), and the non-enhanced tumor (V ne ) were calculated from the ROI all , ROI ce , and ROI ne , respectively. ADC values, including the minimum and maximum ADC of ROI ce (minADC ce , maxADC ce ), the minimum and maximum ADC of ROI ne (minADC ne , maxADC ne ), and the average ADC of ROI all (meanADC all ) were assessed. To account for inter-device differences and whole-brain variations in ADC values among individuals, the relative ADC (rADC) value was defined and calculated by dividing the tumor ADC by the mean ADC value of the normal appearing white matter (NAWM) on the contralateral side of the tumor [20]. e normalization procedure was performed as follows: A circular ROI of 20 mm² was placed in the NAWM of the contralateral corona radiata at the level of the centrum semiovale.
e ROI was carefully positioned to avoid visible vessels, sulci, gray matter interfaces, and any areas of signal abnormality on co-registered T2-FLAIR and CE-T1WI images.

is measurement was performed on three consecutive axial slices, and the final ADC value of NAWM was taken as the average of these three measurements. All ROIs in NAWM were drawn by a single reader to ensure consistency. e rADC values (rminADC ce , rmaxADC ce , rminADC ne , rmaxADC ne , and rmeanADC all ) were then derived by dividing the respective tumor ADC values by this averaged ADC value of NAWM. For each ROI, the average of the measurements from two readers was used as the final value.

div.head: Statistical analysis
div.p: Statistical analysis was performed using Origin (version 2024b) and Python (version 3.7.15, h t t p s : / / w w w . p y t h o n . o r g / ) . p < 0.05 (two-sided) was considered a statistically significant difference. Cohen's kappa statistic (κ) was used to evaluate interobserver agreement for qualitative MRI features, with κ values interpreted as follows: ≤ 0. >0.6 indicating substantial agreement [21].

e intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC) was employed to assess interobserver agreement for the quantitative features, with reproducibility categorized as poor (ICC, 0.00-0.20), fair to good (ICC, 0.40-0.75), or excellent (ICC, >0.75) [22].
e Shapiro-Wilk test was used to test the normality of all continuous quantitative data.

e normally distributed continuous variables are represented by the means ± standard deviations, while non-normally distributed continuous variables are represented by medians and interquartile ranges. Categorical variables are expressed as frequencies. An independent samples t-test was applied to normally distributed continuous variables, and the Mann-Whitney U test was used for non-normally distributed continuous variables. A Chi-square test for categorical variables was used to compare differences in clinical variables and imaging indicators between IDH-mA and IDH-wG. After univariable analysis, the results showed significant differences between IDH-mA and IDH-wG (p < 0.05) were analyzed for multicollinearity. Multicollinearity was assessed by a linear regression model, with the severity quantified by the variance inflation factor (VIF).

e threshold of VIF was set to VIF < 10. VIF < 10 indicated that the collinearity level was within the acceptable range. Significant variables for differentiating between IDH-mA and IDH-wG were selected using univariable logistic regression. Variables of interest in the univariable analysis were included in the multivariable models using backward elimination according to the likelihood ratio with a variable selection criterion of p < 0.05. In the process of selecting the variables, variables with p-value ≥ 0.05 were eliminated step by step. e final retained variables showed statistical significance and low multicollinearity in the logistic regression model. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves and areas under the curve (AUC) were used to evaluate the discrimination performance of the corresponding logistic regression model. Youden's index was used to determine the optimal threshold for calculating accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity. Internal validation was performed using the bootstrap method with resampling 1000 times.

div.head: Patient characteristics
div.p: is study included a total of 189 patients (age range: 21-85 years), comprising 78 females and 111 males. Among the 189 patients, 87 (46.0%) had IDH-mA (57 males [65.5%], age range: 23-72 years), and 102 (54.0%) had IDH-wG (54 males [52.9%], age range: 21-85 years). Of the total patients, 132 (69.8%) patients underwent gross total resection, 34 (18.0%) patients underwent subtotal or partial resection, and 23 (12.2%) patients underwent biopsies. ATRX mutation status was available for only 146 patients; TP53 mutation status was available for only 141 patients. ere was no significant difference in sex, age, molecular markers (ATRX, TP53, Ki-67), or extent of resection between the two groups. e clinical and molecular information of the patients with IDH-mA and IDH-wG are summarized in Table 1.

div.head: Interobserver agreement
div.p: e interobserver agreement for all the imaging features was good to excellent (κ range, 0.841-0.985; ICC range, 0.830-0.928) (Supplementary Table S2).

div.head: Qualitative analysis
div.p: e proportion of multifocality/multicentricity among patients with IDH-mA was lower than that among patients with IDH-wG (13.8% vs. 26.5%, p = 0.032). e incidence of hemorrhage (41.4% vs. 23.5%, p = 0.009) and cortical involvement (96.6% vs. 85.3%, p = 0.009) were significantly higher in the IDH-mA group compared to the IDH-wG group. No significant differences between the two groups were observed in the side of lesion center, pial invasion, ependymal invasion, midline location invasion, and enhancement mode between the two groups.
e qualitative imaging parameters for IDH-mA and IDH-wG are summarized in Table 2 and shown in Fig. 3a. Representative MRI images of IDH-mA and IDH-wG are provided in Fig. 4.

div.head: Comparisons of volume-related and ADC-related metrics between IDH-mA and IDH-wG
div.p: e IDH-mA group exhibited larger V all (p = 0.001) and V ne (p < 0.001) than the IDH-wG group. Compared with IDH-wG, IDH-mA was significantly higher in rmaxADC ce (p < 0.001), rminADC ne (p = 0.015), rmaxADC ne (p = 0.004), and rmeanADC all (p = 0.001). Comparisons of volume-related and ADC-related metrics between IDH-mA and IDH-wG are listed in Table 3. e V all , V ce , V ne , V ce / V all , V ne / V all , rminADC ce , rmaxADC ce , rminADC ne , rmaxADC ne , and rmeanADC all in patients with IDH-mA and IDH-wG are shown in Fig. 3b, c.

div.head: Univariable and multivariable analysis
div.p: In the univariable analysis, age (odds ratio [OR] = 1.02, p = 0.038), multifocality/multicentricity (OR = 0.44, p = 0.034), hemorrhage (OR = 2.29, p = 0.009), cortical involvement (OR = 4.83, p = 0.016), V all (OR = 0.99, p = 0.001), V ne (OR = 0.99, p < 0.001), rmaxADC ce (OR = 0.37, p < 0.001), rmaxADC ne (OR = 0.54, p = 0.007), rminADC ne (OR = 0.41, p = 0.016), and rmeanADC all (OR = 0.39, p = 0.003) were predictors for distinguishing IDH-mA from IDH-wG. Multicollinearity diagnostics revealed no severe collinearity among the candidate variables (all VIFs < 10), ensuring the stability of subsequent regression estimates. Multivariable analysis showed that less multifocality/multicentricity (OR = 2.87, p = 0.033), a larger V ne (OR = 1.02, p = 0.049), and a higher rmaxADC ce (OR = 2.82, p < 0.001) were significantly associated with IDH-mA (Table 4).

e performance of each predictor was presented in Table 5; Fig. 5. e model demonstrated excellent discrimination, with an AUC of 0.849 (95% CI: 0.791-0.908). At the optimal threshold of 0.69, the model achieved an accuracy of 76.5%, with a sensitivity of 66.3% and specificity of 92.3%. For internal validation, we used the bootstrap method to internally validate the model with 1,000 bootstrap resamples, resulting in a mean AUC value of 0.839 (95% CI: 0.681, 0.958), accuracy of 75.4%, sensitivity of 66.6%, and specificity of 86.9% (Fig. 5).

div.head: Discussion
div.p: In this retrospective, single-center cohort study, we discovered differences in both qualitative and quantitative MRI parameters between IDH-mA and IDH-wG. In addition, we constructed a prediction model using logistic regression and identified three variables: multifocality/multicentricity, V ne , and rmaxADC ce . The results demonstrated the model's good discrimination ability with an AUC of 0.849 (95% CI: 0.791-0.908). In addition, it may facilitate non-invasive molecular subtyping for patients with grade 4 adult-type diffuse glioma in accordance with the WHO CNS5 classification.

Despite excluding the neuroimaging features in the WHO CNS5 classification of gliomas, previous studies have demonstrated that neuroimaging can serve a complementary function in determining the molecular status of adult-type diffuse gliomas. For example, the T2-FLAIR mismatch sign has been identified as a specific imaging biomarker for IDH mutations and 1p/19q co-deletion in diffuse low-grade gliomas, albeit with variable sensitivity [23]. is finding suggests a non-invasive method for inferring molecular characteristics, thereby highlighting the potential of neuroimaging to provide supplementary information.

Our study found a significantly higher incidence of multifocal or multicentric tumors in patients with IDH-wG than with IDH-mA (26.5% vs. 13.8%, p = 0.032). Conversely, patients with IDH-mA exhibited a greater incidence of hemorrhage (41.4% vs. 23.5%, p = 0.009) and cortical invasion (96.6% vs. 85.3%, p = 0.009) than those with IDH-wG. Multifocal or multicentric tumors are often associated with more aggressive biological behavior, typically manifesting as a diffusely infiltrating growth pattern. IDH-wG tumors

are characterized by high tumorigenicity and infiltrative migration [24], which predisposes them to spread to adjacent brain tissue, particularly along white matter fiber tracts and subcortical regions. This contributes to a higher prevalence of multifocal or multicentric lesions. Furthermore, common genetic alterations in IDH-wG tumors, such as epidermal growth factor receptor amplification and telomerase reverse transcriptase promoter mutations, are linked to enhanced proliferative capacity and multifocal growth [25,26].

In contrast, IDH-mA tumors exhibit relatively weak angiogenesis, resulting in structurally more fragile blood vessels that are prone to hemorrhage. Additionally, IDH-mutant tumor cells produce the metabolic byproduct (R)-2-hydroxyglutaric acid, which plays a crucial role in vascular pathology. Research indicates that (R)-2-hydroxyglutaric acid can promote endothelial cell proliferation and tube formation, ultimately leading to disorganized, leaky vasculature [27]. This aberrant angiogenesis not only contributes to tumor microenvironment alterations but also increases the risk of intratumoral hemorrhage.

Previous studies have demonstrated significantly lower ADC values in IDH-wildtype tumors than their IDH-mutant counterparts [1,28]. It has been demonstrated that ADC parameters, particularly the rADC, exhibit strong potential in identifying IDH mutation status within the studied cohort, with the ADC ratio of glioblastomas being significantly lower than that of astrocytomas. In our study, nearly all rADC parameters effectively differentiated between IDH-mA and IDH-wG. Notably, rmaxADC ce , rminADC ne , rmaxADC ne , and rmeanADC all were significantly higher in IDH-mA compared to IDH-wG (p < 0.05). This difference may be attributed to the highly mitotic nature of glioblastomas, which exhibit pronounced microstructural alterations, including increased cell density, cellular heterogeneity, hemorrhage, necrosis, and microangiogenesis. Among these features, elevated cell density and cellular heterogeneity considerably restrict water molecule diffusion. In contrast, astrocytomas typically display mild cytosis and nuclear atypia, resulting in relatively less diffusion restriction [29]. Furthermore, IDH-mutant gliomas generally present fewer barriers to tumor spread and lower tissue complexity, characterized by less anatomical invasion, lower cell density, and greater tumor homogeneity. These pathological differences are further supported by the generally lower tissue complexity and fewer diffusion barriers in IDH-mutant gliomas, which characteristically show reduced cellular density, greater homogeneity, and less invasive growth patterns [30]. However, Lazovic et al. [31] found no significant differences in ADC values in non-necrotic tumor regions between patients with IDH-wildtype and those with IDH mutant-type gliomas. This discrepancy may be attributed to variations in patient selection criteria. Our study specifically enrolled only grade 4 adult-type diffuse gliomas classified according to the WHO CNS5 criteria, whereas previous studies included cohorts prior to this updated classification standard.

In terms of tumor volume-related metrics, both V all and V ne measurements were significantly higher in patients with IDH-mA than those with IDH-wG in our study, similar to the previous study [32]. e significantly larger V all and V ne observed in the IDH-mA group can likely be attributed to the tumors' distinct biological characteristics, including metabolic alterations, degree of cellular differentiation, angiogenic capacity, and invasiveness. IDH-mA tumors are characterized by unique molecular profiles that greatly influence their growth dynamics.

ese tumors are molecularly defined by frequent ATRX gene mutations, which promote alternative lengthening of telomeres and consequently facilitate a more diffuse infiltrative growth pattern [33]. IDH-mutant tumors typically exhibit genetic alterations that slow their proliferation rates while simultaneously enhancing their invasiveness, which contributes to the increased tumor volumes. Additionally, IDH-mutant tumors often show a lower infiltration of immune cells with reduced angiogenesis as compared to IDH-wildtype gliomas [34], resulting in smaller enhancing regions and relatively larger V ne .
is phenomenon not only underscores the biological differences between various tumor types but also provides an important imaging basis for clinical diagnosis and treatment.
Our model demonstrated high specificity (92.3%) but relatively modest sensitivity (66.3%).

is implies that when the model classifies a tumor as IDH-wG, it is highly reliable, which could help in prioritizing aggressive treatment strategies or invasive diagnostic procedures for these patients. Conversely, the lower sensitivity suggests that a proportion of IDH-mA may be missed, potentially leading to delayed molecular confirmation or less aggressive initial management. In clinical practice, such a model may serve as a valuable triage tool, particularly in settings where molecular testing is not immediately available or is contraindicated. Future efforts to enhance sensitivity by integrating additional imaging sequences or relevant clinical variables may further augment the model's utility in guiding preoperative decision-making.
A notable strength of our study is the detailed analysis enhanced and non-enhanced tumor regions achieved through tumor segmentation.

is method has allowed for a more comprehensive understanding of the variability and complexity characteristics of heterogeneous tumors. Additionally, we utilized MRI images from various scanners to enhance the robustness of our findings. To reduce potential biases in ADC measurements, we normalized the ADC values to the normal white matter area of the corona radiata on the contralateral side of the tumor. However, our study has several limitations. First, the retrospective and single-center design of our study may introduce selection bias and limit the generalizability of our findings. erefore, future multi-center prospective studies with larger cohorts are warranted to externally validate and refine our model. Second, this study did not evaluate prognostic markers as IDH-mA patients generally demonstrate significantly prolonged survival outcomes, requiring substantially longer follow-up durations for meaningful survival analysis [35]. Finally, it should be noted that the current study was specifically limited to grade 4 gliomas. erefore, additional investigations are warranted to evaluate the model's generalizability to lower-grade gliomas (WHO grades 2-3) or other glioma subtypes.

div.head: Conclusions
div.p: In conclusion, this study has systematically demonstrated that integrative analysis of both qualitative and quantitative MRI features can effectively differentiate between IDH-mA and IDH-wG. By integrating multifocality/multicentricity, V ne , and rmaxADC ce , we developed a predictive model with robust diagnostic performance, providing a clinically practical tool for preoperative molecular stratification. However, further research using larger datasets from multicenter studies is needed to validate these results. In addition, further research is needed to explore the potential of advanced imaging techniques and multi-omics approaches in glioma classification.
